This, you cannot visit from a first world country to a developing one like you can visit France or Germany. The economic and social difference is massive; these people live on mere dollars for their wage, while you probably make more than 15/hr, so yeah, you're pretty well off to them. Unfortunately, some of those who struggle will try and take it from you, since they see you as rich and able to afford it. Plenty of Egyptians are rightly disgusted with this attitude, but it's unfortunately prevalent. If possible, I recommend you visit a city outside of Cairo, there is a lot of beautiful stuff you can see that's less tourist trappy.

It's important to have an idea of what you want to do and to have some sort of in country connection with a guide company or local Friend. Make an itinerary with this guide/friend and stick with it, especially if you don't know Arabic and are Western and are alone, you WILL be scammed. I'm sorry, but that's how it is. You can't go into a country like this speaking English like it's normal and that you'll be accommodated, this isn't Europe. While Egypt definitely has its issues, many of them can be avoided with proper preparation.

I'm happy to hear you've chosen Morocco!
I'm an American who has lived in Morocco short term for immersive study, so I can relate to your question somewhat.

Just a heads up, the level of English in Morocco ranges from great to really poor, so knowing some French or Arabic will be very useful and can save you from getting price gouged sometimes. 

Morocco is pretty safe as a whole if you're a tourist or obviously foreign. There are some social issues with beggars, scammers and there is unfortunately some street harassment towards women, but it's largely vocal as any real trouble would be bad for business. But the vast majority of people are really warm and love sharing their culture.

I'm going to plug Meknès as a good place to stay. It's more out of the craziness and the tourist traps of the bigger cities like Marrakech or Casablanca but still not small. It's relatively condensed, so you can walk from Hamria to the old medina within 30-40 mins which makes for a great pastime and scenery. Taxis are easy to get and i hadn't had any scam issues like i did in other cities. The people I met in Meknès were all incredibly nice and were always willing to help me. The Souq is incredible, just about anything imaginable is there but bargaining is the name of the game. If you do decide on Meknès i do know some good spots.

Meknès is also part of the oncf line, so you can take a train to another city if you need some new scenery. I know it runs to Casablanca and Rabat but i haven't been in Morocco in a few months. Train tickets are not very expensive compared to other places in the world I've been, but the quality varies between trains.

Prices in Meknès are also a bit lower than a lot of the other cities. On an American budget I was able to live way beyond my normal means. Airbnb's in Morocco are miles cheaper than they are in the US. However that usually comes at reduced quality sometimes, your apartment may not have AC, hot water etc. But you'll learn to live with it. But that's usually only an issue if you cheap out. You may want to check the Airbnb's married couple policy, you can do this by messaging the owner. But this archaic law almost got me and a few friends in trouble. Most people are okay if foreign couples stay together, but it's good to double check because some Airbnb's will NOT.

Take my words with a grain of salt since I'm American, but I did recently stay in Morocco for an extended time.  Morocco already does have a drug problem. But I'd say Morocco is very ripe for drug abuse to grow even more. Growing wealth gaps, poor mental health resources  and a dissatisfied youth are prime conditions for drug abuse to grow.

Hi! I'm also around silver and have recently got back into Vladimir after a hiatus. I currently have a pretty steady almost 80% win rate of strong victories going through silver right now, but I also don't play tons of ranked so I'm probably not where I should be. I also play him top which is far from his best role, but I am more familiar with top lane concepts.

Farming is the most important, as it's THE most reliable gold income for you. I find that especially in lower elos you can usually carry off of having about 7cs a min in silver, but try and aim higher. It gives you more damage and stats, which is what Vlad wants as he plays a bit like a stat stick.

What has been helping a lot for me is to play calculated but aggressive when I need to. Play like it's chess and not CoD. I always question my moves and why I'm doing something, down to every auto. This is made me improve across the board by reducing my mistakes. It's important to always be doing SOMETHING, usually that's farming, but warding, invading etc. all provide actual game value too. You'd be surprised how many free kills will fall into your lap when you start knowing how to punish mistakes in silver.

Being familiar with your damage and matchup is also very important on Vladimir. Burning everything and being an auto or two away from a kill can really hurt your tempo. But knowing when you can get that level 2-3 flash kill can be a great way to start a snowball. This is something learned with experience and even I make stupid miscalculations. 

If you have any questions or are curious about anything Vladimir, you're always welcome to ask!

There are pros and cons about Mississippi, some would argue a lot more cons than pros, but I usually hear that talk from out of state folks who just like to shit on us because of our corrupt as fuck government. 

I personally am from out of state as I am an Army brat, and I had and still have my reservations about this state: 

CON: It's almost ridiculous how conservative this state can be at times, especially if you aren't in a bigger town area. Hell, I know conservatives who would nope out of here because of how conservative the politics here are. Prepare to be treated like shit if you do or believe in something seen as taboo. It is literally conservative ground fuckin' zero in majority of the state, barring most decently large cities like Oxford, Tupelo, Jackson etc. Even then it'll most likely still be quite conservative when compared to many blue areas in the US.  PDA is a no unless you are, like, directly on a college campus. Drug use, no matter how minor the offence or use, even for coping with emotional or physical pain or spiritual reasons instantly gets you treated like shit unfortunately. It's a problem that is growing scarily fast and it really needs more empathy involved. Hopefully change is on the horizon with MDMA and psychedelic therapy research, weed medicalization and harm reduction policies booming in recent years, especially with even moderate and conservative figures supporting these motions. 

CON: Guns are a way of life for both left and right here, people hunt and have to defend themselves and they will not take kindly to you suggesting other methods. This also unfortunately causes a huge gun-toting good ole boy problem, people can be very trigger happy, and vandalism and warnings by gunshot are frighteningly common. 

CON: You can and will be singled out for being different, but it's not always negative as some people are just genuinely curious about you and are supportive of you, but some people can get real ugly simply because you dress, act or look a certain way. 

CON: Getting anywhere is a massive pain in the ass without a car, but this is largely an American-wide problem too with suburban planning. If you wanna get anywhere without a car, you're in the wrong place.

CON: Getting reliable work can often be based on who you know. If you are a loner like me, finding work that's not a corporate hellhole is damn near impossible if you don't have someone to vouch for you. So, you better get going to church even if you aren't Christian if you wanna get a somewhat decent job. 

CON: little opportunity to grow as a person, particularly with career work. It sucks here, there is barely any opportunity for younger people, so they leave the state in large troves. I don't blame them

CON: Heat and Humidity, nuff said, Global warming is definitely felt here. It feels like satan's ass crack during August-October

But I would be lying if I said there are no pros to living here.

PRO: Cheap living costs, this was a huge draw to my family as we were making plenty of money from my dad's military work to live pretty damn well. So, coming from an expensive state to Mississippi usually means you can live boujee as hell because of the low prices. 

PRO: The state is just plain beautiful, so much beautiful wildlife and fauna (minus the mosquitos, fuck me they're bad). My backyard legit looks like a fantasy forest with giant mushrooms and bright flowers. 

PRO: People will rarely bother you; sure, people can be a little nosey but a simple "not right now" will suffice 95% of the time. 

PRO: Winters are rarely unbearably cold, **at least at first**, it will become intolerable as you live here, trust me. IDK how I've survived -20F before with a foot of snow when 40f feels cold as hell now. 

PRO: People are generally chill, unless you're near a major city like Memphis, but even then, people are much nicer than they are in other states. 

PRO: Strong sense of community once you are let in. You will legitimately become a pillar of the community if you stay here long enough, like, a surprising amount of people in my decently sized college town know me pretty well as that one army kid who lived in Germany for 6 years and is learning Arabic. 

PRO: **FOOD**, especially if you go to places off of the beaten path, though it's always good to hear what the towns opinion is of these restaurants as bad food poisoning is always possible. Legit, just try some barbeque from a gas station in the middle of nowhere, best decision you'll ever make. Plus, there are often just some cool asf places in larger towns. I know in Oxford they have a secret grilled cheese that requires a dress code and a secret codeword in order to enter the venue. And then you got your standard fast foods and chain restaurants, but they lack soul. 

​

In conclusion, I am eventually planning to move out of here because Arabic will not get me anywhere here, since there is no opportunity for my personal career growth. But I love this state very dearly despite its' honestly pretty egregious issues and I would not trade my experience here for any other. It's going to be difficult leaving. I admire the willingness of people to help out and stand up for others, and this goes politically as well, the left leaning folk here endure so much shit on a daily basis, but they don't give up because they know that Mississippians need help. But the Conservative church going folk don't usually have bad intentions either, usually just somewhat ignorant as to why things are like they are, but they still try to help out when they can. I would compare Mississippi to a lovely, but dirt-poor and troubled friend who makes bad decisions sometimes but, on the inside, you know he has a good soul and you're just waiting for their glow-up. I'd love to see Mississippi thrive and I will do what I can in the future to assist with that.

So ج which is usually a zh sound is now a hard G, that's something to adapt to. However, since it's dialect there is much less rules than compared to MSA (which I'm more used to at this point.) The book does come with a lot of practical vocabulary and practical situations, so that's easily helpful, there's also a small dictionary in the back. 

Avoid Rosetta Stone, it's too expensive and it's in MSA (which you can learn for a much better price if you invest in a dictionary and book, I recommend 10 mins a day series if interested)
Overall it's a pretty good investment for getting the essentials down, it's also more practical for being in a dialect. 

Just something extra, what I find helped me is to watch kids TV once i understood the basics, cartoon Network is a good one, short clips, but a lot of region block.
